Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.

California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20other%20insurers%20have%20stopped%20selling%2C%E2%80%9D%20said%20Amy%20Bach%2C%20executive%20director%20of%20United%20Policyholders%2C%20a%20consumer%20group.%20%E2%80%9CIf%20you%20talk%20to%20an%20agent%20or%20broker%20today%2C%20they%E2%80%99re%20going%20to%20tell%20you%20it%20can%20be%20pretty%20hard%20to%20find%20insurance%E2%80%9D%20outside%20of%20the%20FAIR%20plan%2C%20Bach%20said.%C2%A0) where new homes are being built which has statewide ramifications. California’s state-run insurer of last resort, known as the FAIR Plan, is likely to be overburdened (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=As%20the%20risk%20of%20catastrophic%20wildfire%20ramps%20up%20across%20California%2C%20that%20risk%20falls%20disproportionately%20on%20the%20FAIR%20Plan.) to the extent that more insurers drop coverage across the state.
While home insurance challenges are not unique to Prop. 37, they remain acute in the wildland-urban interface — where almost 45% of the houses built in California have been located (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=Between%201990%20and,in%20the%20state.) over the last 30 years. Though these areas tend to have less expensive real estate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CPeople%20are%20looking%20to%20the%20(wildland%2Durban%20interface)%20as%20one%20of%20the%20only%20places%20that%20has%20capacity%20for%20housing%2C%E2%80%9D%20she%20said.%20Though%20the%20wildland%2Durban%20interface%20includes%20toney%20enclaves%20of%20wealth%20like%20Pacific%20Palisades%2C%20it%20also%20features%20some%20of%20the%20more%20affordable%20real%20estate%20left%20in%20the%20state.), they are also particularly susceptible to wildfires. That exposure could mean higher premiums, more difficulty securing a loan, or dependence on the FAIR Plan, driving additional costs on top of the repayments of Prop. 37.
Altogether, these compounding factors could undercut the affordability gains the measure is purported to provide for Californians. As a result, the benefits of Prop. 37 may skew toward eligible families with greater financial resources who were already better positioned to cover the costs of homeownership.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
There have been some official supporters (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)#google_vignette:~:text=Who%20supports%20and%20opposes%20the%20initiative%3F) of the initiative, but no official opponents as of mid-summer 2026. Former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Robert Hertzberg is the primary sponsor and a supporter of this proposition. Hertzberg has stated the main goal of the measure is to allow working families and their children to build wealth and remain in California (https://www.planningreport.com/2025/10/01/keeping-our-children-california-hertzberg-middle-class-homeownership-act).
Various carpentry-focused unions and realty organizations — like the California Association of Realtors and the Northern California Carpenters Regional Council — have also expressed support for the measure. Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra has also expressed support for this measure.

Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers’ hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California’s housing crisis. But these two measures aren’t it.
We can’t solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Summary
Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE. Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs.

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Proposition 37 would create a homebuyer assistance program with three main
provisions.1 First, the measure authorizes California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to sell
up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund loans covering up to seventeen percent of a qualifying
home’s purchase price, with homeowners’ payments on those loans repaying the bonds and
covering the program’s administrative costs.2 Second, the measure requires buyers to be
California residents with household incomes no greater than 200 percent of their county’s area
median income, and requires eligible homes to meet specified requirements, including a price
limit of no more than $1.5 million and a requirement that the buyer be the first purchaser of the
home.3 Third, the measure allows developers to participate in a “qualified builder option,”
allowing developers who agree to meet higher labor standards to operate under different
construction-defect rules, providing them with greater flexibility in addressing any construction
defect complaints that may arise under the program.4
A “YES” vote on this measure means the state would create a new homebuying
assistance program. Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in state revenue bonds,
repaid through homeowners’ loan payments, and allow qualified builders meeting specified
requirements to elect modified construction-defect standards.5
A “NO” vote on this measure means the state would not be required to create a new
homebuying assistance program.6
II. THE LAW
A. Historical Background on California’s Housing Crisis
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development generally defines housing as
affordable when an occupant pays no more than thirty percent of his or her monthly income for
housing costs, including utilities.7 When a homeowner or renter pays more than thirty percent of
their monthly income for housing, they are considered “housing cost-burdened.”8 When they pay
over fifty percent of their monthly income for housing, they are considered “severely cost-
burdened.”9

In 1970, fifty-five percent of California households owned their homes.10 For those who
rented, two-thirds of them lived in affordable homes.11 However, this began to change during the
1970s.12 The share of California renters who paid an unaffordable percentage of their income on
rent and utilities dramatically increased.13 Compared to 1970, nearly four times as many
Californians are severely rent burdened, spending over fifty percent of their income on housing
costs.14
Today, California has the second lowest homeownership rate in the nation.15 For renter
households, over half are cost burdened and over a quarter are severely cost burdened.16 For
homeowners with mortgages, over a third are cost burdened.17 Unaffordable housing costs also
disproportionately affect people of color in California.18 Over two-thirds of people who are
housing cost burdened are people of color. 19
B. California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA)
The CalHFA was created in 1975 through the passage of the Zenovich–Moscone–Chacon
Housing and Home Finance Act.20 The agency was created to help address the housing crisis by
financing affordable rental housing.21 The agency works with developers as well as local, state,
and federal government partners.22 CalHFA also helps provide first-time homebuyers with down
payments, closing cost assistance, and access to first mortgage loans.23 The state agency is self-
supported and does not rely on taxpayers dollars for its operational costs.24 It does, however,
regularly administer various state and federal resources on the state’s behalf.25

D. Revenue Bonds
Revenue bonds are a separate category of state borrowing. As with GO bonds, the state
sells revenue bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for a public project, and investors are
repaid over time with interest.30 The key distinction is in the repayment source: revenue bonds
are intended to be repaid using revenues generated by the project itself, such as fees or other
payments by the project’s users, rather than from the state’s General Fund.31
E. Proposition 37 Bonds
Proposition 37 would authorize CalHFA to use revenue bonds, rather than general
obligation bonds, to finance its home-loan program.32 As a revenue bond, it does not require
voter approval and could have been enacted legislatively or through a similar program
established by CaHFA.33 Because Proposition 37 relies on revenue bonds, repayment is intended
to come from revenues generated by the program itself, namely, homeowners’ payments on their
assisted loans, rather than from the state’s General Fund.34

bonds rather than general obligation bonds, voter approval was not constitutionally required.35
The measure appears on the ballot by virtue of the initiative process, not because the bond type
demanded it.36 Second, because repayment is structurally tied to program revenue rather than the
General Fund, the measure is estimated to result in no direct state or local costs.37 This

5. Qualified Builders
State law establishes minimum standards for residential construction and provides
procedures that homeowners and builders generally must follow before a homeowner may bring
a construction-defect action.57 Proposition 37 preserves those substantive standards but creates
an optional alternative for participating builders.58
All developers can build homes eligible for purchase under the CalHFA program.59 There
is also a qualified builder option, which housing developers may opt into by certifying the
constructions will satisfy the Section 51515.01, subdivision (b) requirements for qualified
homes.60 In exchange, participating builders receive different procedural treatment for certain
construction-defect claims, but are not exempted from Title 7’s underlying substantive
construction standards.61
Qualified builders shall comply with higher labor and enforcement provisions for the
project and construction craft conditions pursuant to Section 21080.66, subdivision (d),
paragraphs (2)-(5) of the Public Resources Code.62 These provisions establish labor protections,
including prevailing-wage requirements for workers on buildings exceeding eighty-five feet in
height and a joint labor-management cooperation committee authorized to bring actions for
specified construction-site violations.63
The modified construction-defect procedures streamline the process for addressing
homeowner claims and provide builders with additional protections following completed
repairs.64 Proposition 37 provides that Title 7 of the Civil Code continues to apply to qualified
new homes, but modifies specified right-to-repair procedures for homes built under the qualified
builder option.65 These modifications include additional notice requirements, direct
communication between builders and homeowners during the repair process, limited releases
following completed repairs, and litigation timing.66
The qualified builder option is also conditional rather than permanent. If a builder sells a
qualified new home built under the option for more than twenty-five percent above the
program’s maximum sale price, the modified construction-defect provisions in section
51515.04(e)(1)(B) no longer apply to that home.67 The preferential treatment is therefore
conditioned on the builder’s continued compliance with the program’s requirements.

6. Consumer Protections
CalHFA shall also establish consumer protection requirements.70 These protections place
limits on lenders fees, prohibit early payment penalties, and require homeownership loans to be
fixed rate mortgages.71 There are also protections that allow for additional credit verification,

III. CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY ISSUES
A. Statutory Interpretation
The proposition is clearly written as a revenue bond measure that allows CalHFA to issue
and sell bonds to be used as a payment assistance program for qualified homes and home
buyers.73
The qualified builder option's labor standards are not defined within Proposition 37 itself.
Instead, the measure incorporates those standards by cross-reference to Public Resources Code
section 21080.66(d), a separate CEQA-streamlining provision that imposes prevailing wage and
skilled-and-trained-workforce requirements on qualifying housing projects.74
The specific requirements vary based on factors such as project height, unit count, and
affordability mix.75 Builders who opt into the program must therefore satisfy the applicable tier
of that external framework in exchange for the modified construction-defect rules the measure
provides.76

B. Constitutional Analysis
1. Bond Authorization
Proposition 37 is structured so that the state is not pledging its taxing power or General
Fund to repay the bonds authorized under the measure.77 On this basis, the measure has a strong
argument that it does not create the type of “debt” that would trigger the constitutional
procedures applicable to state general-obligation debt, since repayment is tied to program
revenue rather than the state's broader taxing authority.78
2. Is Using Public Authority to Finance Private Home Purchases
Constitutional?
Article XVI, section 6 of the California Constitution prohibits gifts of public funds and
the lending of public credit.79 Because Proposition 37 directs CalHFA, a state agency, to provide
loans to individual Californians to help them purchase private homes, the measure raises the
question of whether the state is improperly using public resources for a private purpose.
California law, however, permits public entities to engage in programs that benefit
individuals when those programs serve a legitimate public purpose.80 Proposition 37 expressly
identifies several such purposes; including expanding homeownership opportunities,
encouraging new housing construction, addressing California's shortage of single-family
housing, protecting consumers from unfair lending practices, and promoting investment in
housing.81
Although the individual homeowners receive the immediate benefit of the loans, the
measure identifies broader public objectives that extend beyond those individual recipients.82
Voters approving Proposition 37 would therefore be supporting a program directed towards
housing supply, homeownership, and economic development.83 California courts have generally
recognized that such broader public purposes can support programs that provide incidental
benefits to private individuals against challenges under Article XVI, section 6.84
3. California Constitution Article XVI, Section 1
Article XVI, section 1 separately restricts the Legislature from creating state debt above a
specified constitutional threshold.85 In California Housing Finance Agency v. Elliott,86 the

5. Qualified Builders
State law establishes minimum standards for residential construction and provides
procedures that homeowners and builders generally must follow before a homeowner may bring
a construction-defect action.57 Proposition 37 preserves those substantive standards but creates
an optional alternative for participating builders.58
All developers can build homes eligible for purchase under the CalHFA program.59 There
is also a qualified builder option, which housing developers may opt into by certifying the
constructions will satisfy the Section 51515.01, subdivision (b) requirements for qualified
homes.60 In exchange, participating builders receive different procedural treatment for certain
construction-defect claims, but are not exempted from Title 7’s underlying substantive
construction standards.61
Qualified builders shall comply with higher labor and enforcement provisions for the
project and construction craft conditions pursuant to Section 21080.66, subdivision (d),
paragraphs (2)-(5) of the Public Resources Code.62 These provisions establish labor protections,
including prevailing-wage requirements for workers on buildings exceeding eighty-five feet in
height and a joint labor-management cooperation committee authorized to bring actions for
specified construction-site violations.63
The modified construction-defect procedures streamline the process for addressing
homeowner claims and provide builders with additional protections following completed
repairs.64 Proposition 37 provides that Title 7 of the Civil Code continues to apply to qualified
new homes, but modifies specified right-to-repair procedures for homes built under the qualified
builder option.65 These modifications include additional notice requirements, direct
communication between builders and homeowners during the repair process, limited releases
following completed repairs, and litigation timing.66
The qualified builder option is also conditional rather than permanent. If a builder sells a
qualified new home built under the option for more than twenty-five percent above the
program’s maximum sale price, the modified construction-defect provisions in section
51515.04(e)(1)(B) no longer apply to that home.67 The preferential treatment is therefore
conditioned on the builder’s continued compliance with the program’s requirements.

6. Consumer Protections
CalHFA shall also establish consumer protection requirements.70 These protections place
limits on lenders fees, prohibit early payment penalties, and require homeownership loans to be
fixed rate mortgages.71 There are also protections that allow for additional credit verification,
hardship deferrals of monthly interest payments, and construction accountability standards which
include right-to-repair procedures.72
III. CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY ISSUES
A. Statutory Interpretation
The proposition is clearly written as a revenue bond measure that allows CalHFA to issue
and sell bonds to be used as a payment assistance program for qualified homes and home
buyers.73
The qualified builder option's labor standards are not defined within Proposition 37 itself.
Instead, the measure incorporates those standards by cross-reference to Public Resources Code
section 21080.66(d), a separate CEQA-streamlining provision that imposes prevailing wage and
skilled-and-trained-workforce requirements on qualifying housing projects.74
The specific requirements vary based on factors such as project height, unit count, and
affordability mix.75 Builders who opt into the program must therefore satisfy the applicable tier
of that external framework in exchange for the modified construction-defect rules the measure
provides.76

B. Constitutional Analysis
1. Bond Authorization
Proposition 37 is structured so that the state is not pledging its taxing power or General
Fund to repay the bonds authorized under the measure.77 On this basis, the measure has a strong
argument that it does not create the type of “debt” that would trigger the constitutional
procedures applicable to state general-obligation debt, since repayment is tied to program
revenue rather than the state's broader taxing authority.78
2. Is Using Public Authority to Finance Private Home Purchases
Constitutional?
Article XVI, section 6 of the California Constitution prohibits gifts of public funds and
the lending of public credit.79 Because Proposition 37 directs CalHFA, a state agency, to provide
loans to individual Californians to help them purchase private homes, the measure raises the
question of whether the state is improperly using public resources for a private purpose.
California law, however, permits public entities to engage in programs that benefit
individuals when those programs serve a legitimate public purpose.80 Proposition 37 expressly
identifies several such purposes; including expanding homeownership opportunities,
encouraging new housing construction, addressing California's shortage of single-family
housing, protecting consumers from unfair lending practices, and promoting investment in
housing.81
Although the individual homeowners receive the immediate benefit of the loans, the
measure identifies broader public objectives that extend beyond those individual recipients.82
Voters approving Proposition 37 would therefore be supporting a program directed towards
housing supply, homeownership, and economic development.83 California courts have generally
recognized that such broader public purposes can support programs that provide incidental
benefits to private individuals against challenges under Article XVI, section 6.84
3. California Constitution Article XVI, Section 1
Article XVI, section 1 separately restricts the Legislature from creating state debt above a
specified constitutional threshold.85 In California Housing Finance Agency v. Elliott,86 the

“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.

“In concept, [Proposition 37 is] a great idea,” Lewis said. “The thing we’re concerned about is, California is still way behind on its housing production goals, so there’s the risk of an unintended consequence of instead of having 10 people bidding on a house, now you’ve given a couple folks down payment assistance, and so there’s now 12 people bidding on the same house.”
To drive builders to construct eligible homes, the measure would allow them to opt into a “qualified builder” option. As long as they adhere to price caps, agree to certain labor requirements and fix repairs that arise, they’re protected from lawsuits from buyers concerning defects 10 years after construction of the home.
Homebuilders say even given some relief from litigation, they aren’t sure Proposition 37 would push construction into overdrive.
Advertisement
“There are so many more things the state, city and county could do to help add more supply [of homes],” said Paul Schon, a developer who builds apartments in L.A. County. He said tackling permitting times and red tape involved in building would have a greater impact. “This is minor,” he said.
Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.

One of the biggest financial backers of the measure is the political nonprofit Building a Better California, which has been fighting the billionaire’s tax with help from wealthy donors (https://www.latimes.com/business/story/2026-08-12/googles-sergey-brin-spent-102-million-fighting-california-wealth-tax), including Google co-founder Sergey Brin.
Hertzberg, for his part, refused to name any organization or person who may be interested in buying the bonds that would fund this program.

California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20other%20insurers%20have%20stopped%20selling%2C%E2%80%9D%20said%20Amy%20Bach%2C%20executive%20director%20of%20United%20Policyholders%2C%20a%20consumer%20group.%20%E2%80%9CIf%20you%20talk%20to%20an%20agent%20or%20broker%20today%2C%20they%E2%80%99re%20going%20to%20tell%20you%20it%20can%20be%20pretty%20hard%20to%20find%20insurance%E2%80%9D%20outside%20of%20the%20FAIR%20plan%2C%20Bach%20said.%C2%A0) where new homes are being built which has statewide ramifications. California’s state-run insurer of last resort, known as the FAIR Plan, is likely to be overburdened (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=As%20the%20risk%20of%20catastrophic%20wildfire%20ramps%20up%20across%20California%2C%20that%20risk%20falls%20disproportionately%20on%20the%20FAIR%20Plan.) to the extent that more insurers drop coverage across the state.
While home insurance challenges are not unique to Prop. 37, they remain acute in the wildland-urban interface — where almost 45% of the houses built in California have been located (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=Between%201990%20and,in%20the%20state.) over the last 30 years. Though these areas tend to have less expensive real estate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CPeople%20are%20looking%20to%20the%20(wildland%2Durban%20interface)%20as%20one%20of%20the%20only%20places%20that%20has%20capacity%20for%20housing%2C%E2%80%9D%20she%20said.%20Though%20the%20wildland%2Durban%20interface%20includes%20toney%20enclaves%20of%20wealth%20like%20Pacific%20Palisades%2C%20it%20also%20features%20some%20of%20the%20more%20affordable%20real%20estate%20left%20in%20the%20state.), they are also particularly susceptible to wildfires. That exposure could mean higher premiums, more difficulty securing a loan, or dependence on the FAIR Plan, driving additional costs on top of the repayments of Prop. 37.
Altogether, these compounding factors could undercut the affordability gains the measure is purported to provide for Californians. As a result, the benefits of Prop. 37 may skew toward eligible families with greater financial resources who were already better positioned to cover the costs of homeownership.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
There have been some official supporters (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)#google_vignette:~:text=Who%20supports%20and%20opposes%20the%20initiative%3F) of the initiative, but no official opponents as of mid-summer 2026. Former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Robert Hertzberg is the primary sponsor and a supporter of this proposition. Hertzberg has stated the main goal of the measure is to allow working families and their children to build wealth and remain in California (https://www.planningreport.com/2025/10/01/keeping-our-children-california-hertzberg-middle-class-homeownership-act).
Various carpentry-focused unions and realty organizations — like the California Association of Realtors and the Northern California Carpenters Regional Council — have also expressed support for the measure. Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra has also expressed support for this measure.

Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers’ hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California’s housing crisis. But these two measures aren’t it.
We can’t solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. **Assessing legal issues**

I’m looking into a pivotal matter involving law around construction arbitration fee caps and wages, especially regarding existing loans. It seems necessary to analyze whether claims about bond defaults and related risks to CalHFA funds are accurate. There's no clear user values stated, and I must decide on a yes/no basis based on merits, not policy restrictions. This ballot measure includes buyers' loans, tort reforms for builders, and agency regulations. I’ll need to dive deep into legal and legislative analysis while exploring comparative rates too.**Evaluating taxpayer implications**

I need to consider that not automatically stating zero cost to taxpayers has an opportunity cost at the program scale, factoring in externalities and consumer protections. The KQED wording contradicts the LAO, so I should discard that. Regarding claims of "no cost to taxpayers," fees like tax-exempt bonds might lead to borrower payments, while Prop 37 introduces a new voluntary credit option. However, its value is uncertain, as borrowers can refuse if worse than market rates. I must analyze how this debt affects down payments and compare it with traditional mortgage options.**Analyzing mortgage claims**

Critics argue that adding a second mortgage suggests an increase in principal. However, the debt level remains comparable to loans that cover 97% loan-to-value. The second mortgage reduces the first mortgage principal from 97% to 80%, so it's misleading to say there's simply more debt if the down payment is low. Also, the existing CalHFA silent second mortgage at 1% interest is more favorable for qualified buyers, but it's state-financed with stricter eligibility. This new program could help the missing middle without costing taxpayers.

Proposition 37:
California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home
Construction Act of 2026
Bond Initiative
Copyright © 2026 by the University of the Pacific, McGeorge School of Law
By
Siena Giampaoli
J.D., University of the Pacific, McGeorge School of Law, to be conferred 2028
B.A., Psychology and Religious Studies, Gonzaga University, 2024
&
Sara Walling
J.D., University of the Pacific, McGeorge School of Law, to be conferred 2027
B.A., Government, California State University, Sacramento, 2012
1
I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY
Proposition 37 would create a homebuyer assistance program with three main
provisions.1 First, the measure authorizes California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA) to sell
up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund loans covering up to seventeen percent of a qualifying
home’s purchase price, with homeowners’ payments on those loans repaying the bonds and
covering the program’s administrative costs.2 Second, the measure requires buyers to be
California residents with household incomes no greater than 200 percent of their county’s area
median income, and requires eligible homes to meet specified requirements, including a price
limit of no more than $1.5 million and a requirement that the buyer be the first purchaser of the
home.3 Third, the measure allows developers to participate in a “qualified builder option,”
allowing developers who agree to meet higher labor standards to operate under different
construction-defect rules, providing them with greater flexibility in addressing any construction
defect complaints that may arise under the program.4
A “YES” vote on this measure means the state would create a new homebuying
assistance program. Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in state revenue bonds,
repaid through homeowners’ loan payments, and allow qualified builders meeting specified
requirements to elect modified construction-defect standards.5
A “NO” vote on this measure means the state would not be required to create a new
homebuying assistance program.6
II. THE LAW
A. Historical Background on California’s Housing Crisis
The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development generally defines housing as
affordable when an occupant pays no more than thirty percent of his or her monthly income for
housing costs, including utilities.7 When a homeowner or renter pays more than thirty percent of
their monthly income for housing, they are considered “housing cost-burdened.”8 When they pay
over fifty percent of their monthly income for housing, they are considered “severely cost-
burdened.”9
1 Cal. Proposition 37, § 2, (2026) https://perma.cc/P94F-F97J.
2 Id.
3 Id.
4 Cal. Legis. Analyst’s Off., Proposition 37: Creates Loan Program for Middle-Income Buyers of Qualified New
Homes. Initiative Statute., (Nov. 3, 2026), at 1, https://perma.cc/58LK-WX7Z.
5 Id.
6 Id.
7 U.S. Dep’t of Hous. & Urb. Dev., Glossary of HUD Terms, https://perma.cc/JZ5G-DKHB.
8 Id.
9 Id.
2
In 1970, fifty-five percent of California households owned their homes.10 For those who
rented, two-thirds of them lived in affordable homes.11 However, this began to change during the
1970s.12 The share of California renters who paid an unaffordable percentage of their income on
rent and utilities dramatically increased.13 Compared to 1970, nearly four times as many
Californians are severely rent burdened, spending over fifty percent of their income on housing
costs.14
Today, California has the second lowest homeownership rate in the nation.15 For renter
households, over half are cost burdened and over a quarter are severely cost burdened.16 For
homeowners with mortgages, over a third are cost burdened.17 Unaffordable housing costs also
disproportionately affect people of color in California.18 Over two-thirds of people who are
housing cost burdened are people of color. 19
B. California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA)
The CalHFA was created in 1975 through the passage of the Zenovich–Moscone–Chacon
Housing and Home Finance Act.20 The agency was created to help address the housing crisis by
financing affordable rental housing.21 The agency works with developers as well as local, state,
and federal government partners.22 CalHFA also helps provide first-time homebuyers with down
payments, closing cost assistance, and access to first mortgage loans.23 The state agency is self-
supported and does not rely on taxpayers dollars for its operational costs.24 It does, however,
regularly administer various state and federal resources on the state’s behalf.25
C. General Obligation (GO) Bonds
When the state finances a project through bonds rather than paying up front with funds it
already has, the total cost of the project increases, because the state must also pay interest on the
10 Gender Equity Pol’y Inst., The Origins of California’s Housing Crisis: Fifty Years of Rising Housing Costs and
the Unequal Impacts on Californians (June 2024), https://perma.cc/C59V-J6WX.
11 Id.
12 Id.
13 Id.
14 Id.
15 Marisol Cuellar Mejia, Hans Johnson & Julien Lafortune, California’s Housing Divide, Pub. Pol’y Inst. of Cal.
(Oct. 21, 2024), https://perma.cc/MAG7-PNMS.
16 Sara Kimberlin, California’s Housing Affordability Crisis: Renters and Households With the Lowest Incomes are
Hit the Hardest, Cal. Budget & Pol’y Ctr. (Apr. 2019), https://perma.cc/G9NH-U9YQ.
17 Id.
18 Id.
19 Id.
20 Cal. Health & Safety Code § 50000 (2026).
21 Id.
22 Cal. Hous. Fin. Agency, About Us, https://perma.cc/F52L-77YJ.

borrowed amount.26 The size of that additional cost depends on the interest rate secured and the
length of time it takes to repay the debt.27 The California Constitution requires that most new
bonds receive voter approval, and general obligation bonds are typically repaid from the state’s
General Fund: the same account the state draws on to pay for most public services, including
education, health care, and prisons.28 As of 2026, California is already carrying roughly $80
billion in outstanding General Fund-supported bond debt, and the state pays approximately $6.3
billion per year from the General Fund toward repaying that debt, out of $8.2 billion in total debt
service from all funds.29
D. Revenue Bonds
Revenue bonds are a separate category of state borrowing. As with GO bonds, the state
sells revenue bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for a public project, and investors are
repaid over time with interest.30 The key distinction is in the repayment source: revenue bonds
are intended to be repaid using revenues generated by the project itself, such as fees or other
payments by the project’s users, rather than from the state’s General Fund.31
E. Proposition 37 Bonds
Proposition 37 would authorize CalHFA to use revenue bonds, rather than general
obligation bonds, to finance its home-loan program.32 As a revenue bond, it does not require
voter approval and could have been enacted legislatively or through a similar program
established by CaHFA.33 Because Proposition 37 relies on revenue bonds, repayment is intended
to come from revenues generated by the program itself, namely, homeowners’ payments on their
assisted loans, rather than from the state’s General Fund.34
This distinction matters for two reasons. First, because the measure authorizes revenue
bonds rather than general obligation bonds, voter approval was not constitutionally required.35
The measure appears on the ballot by virtue of the initiative process, not because the bond type
demanded it.36 Second, because repayment is structurally tied to program revenue rather than the
General Fund, the measure is estimated to result in no direct state or local costs.37 This

28 Cal. Legis. Analyst’s Off. Bonds, https://perma.cc/2RZG-2XS5.
29 Cal. Legis. Analyst’s Off. Bonds, supra note 28; Cal. Legis Analyst’s Off. The 2026-27 Spending Plan: Other
Provisions, https://perma.cc/VMM6-G62H.

distinguishes Proposition 37 from the roughly $80 billion in General Fund-supported bond debt
the state is already carrying.
The allocation of losses from borrower defaults remains unclear. CalHFA may collect
overdue payments, enforce mortgages, pledge loans as collateral, and establish reserves or obtain
credit enhancements.38 However, the measure does not specify whether these protections would
fully cover default-related losses.39 Because the bonds are not backed by the state’s general
credit, bondholders could bear any remaining losses if loan defaults leave CalHFA without
sufficient funds to meet its bond obligations.40
F. Pathway to the Ballot
Proposition 37 is a bond proposal authored by former state Senate Majority Leader and
California Assembly Speaker Bob Hertzberg.41 Sen. Hertzberg co-authored SB 1457, the
California Family Home Construction and Homeownership Bond Act of 2022.42 The bill would
have authorized the issuance of $25 billion in General Obligation bonds to the CalHFA to assist
with the downpayment or closing costs for the purchase of a new home.43 However, the bill
failed to pass and former Sen. Hertzberg noted he “couldn’t get something just focused on the
middle class” through the legislative process, which prompted him to go through the citizen
initiative process.44
G. Proposition 37: California Middle-Class Home Ownership and Family Home
Construction Act of 202645
1. Additions to Existing Statute
Proposition 37 would add a new section, Chapter 11.5, to Part 3 of Division 31 of the
Health and Safety Code.46
2. Proposal
The CalHFA shall administer and implement Proposition 37 to sell up to $25 billion in
revenue bonds.47 The bonds would be used to establish middle-class home ownership loans to
create a down payment assistance program for eligible borrowers.48 Homeowners would need to

40 Id.

(Aug. 23, 2026), https://perma.cc/9NXL-QQZ5.

provide at least three percent down payment and each loan would cover up to seventeen percent
of the home’s purchase price.49
3. Borrower Eligibility
Eligible borrowers must satisfy Section 51515.01, subdivision (a) to be eligible for the
home ownership loans.50 A borrower must 1) be a resident of California for at least one year, 2)
shall agree to occupy the home as the applicant’s primary residence within sixty days of closing,
3) shall have a family income that does not exceed 200 percent of the area median income, and
4) shall agree to pay no less than three percent of the home’s purchase price.51
4. New Home Eligibility
Qualified new homes are single-family homes that satisfy the requirements established in
51515.01, subdivision (b), which includes, but is not limited to, the qualified builder option
established in Section 51515.02.52 To be a qualified as a new home, it must be 1) a newly
constructed home, townhome, row house, condominium, or manufactured home where the
borrower is the first purchaser, or 2) a condominium or other residential unit in a building that
was a nonresidential structure and was retrofitted or repurposed for residential use where the
borrower is the first purchaser.53 The maximum sales price shall not exceed 125 percent of the
conforming loan limit for a one-unit property (a single-family home) in the county where the
home is located.54

5. Qualified Builders
State law establishes minimum standards for residential construction and provides
procedures that homeowners and builders generally must follow before a homeowner may bring
a construction-defect action.57 Proposition 37 preserves those substantive standards but creates
an optional alternative for participating builders.58
All developers can build homes eligible for purchase under the CalHFA program.59 There
is also a qualified builder option, which housing developers may opt into by certifying the
constructions will satisfy the Section 51515.01, subdivision (b) requirements for qualified
homes.60 In exchange, participating builders receive different procedural treatment for certain
construction-defect claims, but are not exempted from Title 7’s underlying substantive
construction standards.61
Qualified builders shall comply with higher labor and enforcement provisions for the
project and construction craft conditions pursuant to Section 21080.66, subdivision (d),
paragraphs (2)-(5) of the Public Resources Code.62 These provisions establish labor protections,
including prevailing-wage requirements for workers on buildings exceeding eighty-five feet in
height and a joint labor-management cooperation committee authorized to bring actions for
specified construction-site violations.63
The modified construction-defect procedures streamline the process for addressing
homeowner claims and provide builders with additional protections following completed
repairs.64 Proposition 37 provides that Title 7 of the Civil Code continues to apply to qualified
new homes, but modifies specified right-to-repair procedures for homes built under the qualified
builder option.65 These modifications include additional notice requirements, direct
communication between builders and homeowners during the repair process, limited releases
following completed repairs, and litigation timing.66
The qualified builder option is also conditional rather than permanent. If a builder sells a
qualified new home built under the option for more than twenty-five percent above the
program’s maximum sale price, the modified construction-defect provisions in section
51515.04(e)(1)(B) no longer apply to that home.67 The preferential treatment is therefore
conditioned on the builder’s continued compliance with the program’s requirements.

III. CONSTITUTIONAL AND STATUTORY ISSUES
A. Statutory Interpretation
The proposition is clearly written as a revenue bond measure that allows CalHFA to issue
and sell bonds to be used as a payment assistance program for qualified homes and home
buyers.73
The qualified builder option's labor standards are not defined within Proposition 37 itself.
Instead, the measure incorporates those standards by cross-reference to Public Resources Code
section 21080.66(d), a separate CEQA-streamlining provision that imposes prevailing wage and
skilled-and-trained-workforce requirements on qualifying housing projects.74
The specific requirements vary based on factors such as project height, unit count, and
affordability mix.75 Builders who opt into the program must therefore satisfy the applicable tier
of that external framework in exchange for the modified construction-defect rules the measure
provides.76

B. Constitutional Analysis
1. Bond Authorization
Proposition 37 is structured so that the state is not pledging its taxing power or General
Fund to repay the bonds authorized under the measure.77 On this basis, the measure has a strong
argument that it does not create the type of “debt” that would trigger the constitutional
procedures applicable to state general-obligation debt, since repayment is tied to program
revenue rather than the state's broader taxing authority.78
2. Is Using Public Authority to Finance Private Home Purchases
Constitutional?
Article XVI, section 6 of the California Constitution prohibits gifts of public funds and
the lending of public credit.79 Because Proposition 37 directs CalHFA, a state agency, to provide
loans to individual Californians to help them purchase private homes, the measure raises the
question of whether the state is improperly using public resources for a private purpose.
California law, however, permits public entities to engage in programs that benefit
individuals when those programs serve a legitimate public purpose.80 Proposition 37 expressly
identifies several such purposes; including expanding homeownership opportunities,
encouraging new housing construction, addressing California's shortage of single-family
housing, protecting consumers from unfair lending practices, and promoting investment in
housing.81
Although the individual homeowners receive the immediate benefit of the loans, the
measure identifies broader public objectives that extend beyond those individual recipients.82
Voters approving Proposition 37 would therefore be supporting a program directed towards
housing supply, homeownership, and economic development.83 California courts have generally
recognized that such broader public purposes can support programs that provide incidental
benefits to private individuals against challenges under Article XVI, section 6.84
3. California Constitution Article XVI, Section 1

specified constitutional threshold.85 In California Housing Finance Agency v. Elliott,86 the

Interest rates could be a tough sell
Many down payment assistance programs offer interest-free loans to homebuyers, including an existing program run by CalHFA.
But in order to be self-funding, the fixed-rate loans offered through Proposition 37 would carry interest. If passed, the state would issue revenue bonds, selling them to investors and using that money to issue loans to homebuyers. The investors are repaid with the interest paid on the loans.
According to the Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=37&year=2026), CalHFA would decide the total amount of bonds to issue and over what period of time.
Revenue bonds are generally viewed as riskier than other types of government bonds, in part because they’re backed by the promise of revenue from a specific project (https://www.msrb.org/Sources-Repayment) — in this case, payment by individual borrowers. That means interest rates on these loans could be higher than borrowers might like or be able to afford.
Hertzberg said he’s talked to investors who may be willing to buy these bonds at cheaper rates, given the crushing issue the funding is trying to solve. This would keep interest rates down for borrowers. He said he’s appealing to foundations and socially-minded tech leaders.

California’s home insurance market also compounds the problem. Some state insurers have stopped providing coverage in many of the wildfire-prone areas (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CA%20lot%20of%20other%20insurers%20have%20stopped%20selling%2C%E2%80%9D%20said%20Amy%20Bach%2C%20executive%20director%20of%20United%20Policyholders%2C%20a%20consumer%20group.%20%E2%80%9CIf%20you%20talk%20to%20an%20agent%20or%20broker%20today%2C%20they%E2%80%99re%20going%20to%20tell%20you%20it%20can%20be%20pretty%20hard%20to%20find%20insurance%E2%80%9D%20outside%20of%20the%20FAIR%20plan%2C%20Bach%20said.%C2%A0) where new homes are being built which has statewide ramifications. California’s state-run insurer of last resort, known as the FAIR Plan, is likely to be overburdened (https://calmatters.org/housing/2023/05/state-farm-california-insurance/#:~:text=As%20the%20risk%20of%20catastrophic%20wildfire%20ramps%20up%20across%20California%2C%20that%20risk%20falls%20disproportionately%20on%20the%20FAIR%20Plan.) to the extent that more insurers drop coverage across the state.
While home insurance challenges are not unique to Prop. 37, they remain acute in the wildland-urban interface — where almost 45% of the houses built in California have been located (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=Between%201990%20and,in%20the%20state.) over the last 30 years. Though these areas tend to have less expensive real estate (https://calmatters.org/housing/2025/01/ca-wui-housing-policy/#:~:text=%E2%80%9CPeople%20are%20looking%20to%20the%20(wildland%2Durban%20interface)%20as%20one%20of%20the%20only%20places%20that%20has%20capacity%20for%20housing%2C%E2%80%9D%20she%20said.%20Though%20the%20wildland%2Durban%20interface%20includes%20toney%20enclaves%20of%20wealth%20like%20Pacific%20Palisades%2C%20it%20also%20features%20some%20of%20the%20more%20affordable%20real%20estate%20left%20in%20the%20state.), they are also particularly susceptible to wildfires. That exposure could mean higher premiums, more difficulty securing a loan, or dependence on the FAIR Plan, driving additional costs on top of the repayments of Prop. 37.
Altogether, these compounding factors could undercut the affordability gains the measure is purported to provide for Californians. As a result, the benefits of Prop. 37 may skew toward eligible families with greater financial resources who were already better positioned to cover the costs of homeownership.
Who Supports and Opposes Prop. 37?
There have been some official supporters (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_37,_Second_Mortgage_Homebuyer_Program_and_Revenue_Bond_Initiative_(2026)#google_vignette:~:text=Who%20supports%20and%20opposes%20the%20initiative%3F) of the initiative, but no official opponents as of mid-summer 2026. Former California Senate Majority Leader and Assembly Speaker Robert Hertzberg is the primary sponsor and a supporter of this proposition. Hertzberg has stated the main goal of the measure is to allow working families and their children to build wealth and remain in California (https://www.planningreport.com/2025/10/01/keeping-our-children-california-hertzberg-middle-class-homeownership-act).
Various carpentry-focused unions and realty organizations — like the California Association of Realtors and the Northern California Carpenters Regional Council — have also expressed support for the measure. Gubernatorial candidate Xavier Becerra has also expressed support for this measure.

tion as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.
But Proposition 37 would give future builders an escape hatch, if not a bonanza. Instead of having to lower prices, it could artificially inflate the market by putting (borrowed) cash into buyers’ hands.
No wonder realtors, carpenters and builders are throwing money to get this passed.
There is a role for government to play in California’s housing crisis. But these two measures aren’t it.
We can’t solve our way out by pumping more money into a broken system and calling creative ways to finance more debt the solution.
Reject Propositions 1 and 37.

Proposition 37
Create low-cost mortgages for homebuyers
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

Support
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Oppose
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

# Code Section
## Code Text
#### CHAPTER 2. Mortgage [2920 - 2968]
##### ARTICLE 1. Mortgages in General [2920 - 2944.10]
###### 2924.13.
(a) As used in this section:
(1) “Borrower” has the same meaning as defined in Section 2929.5.
(2) “Mortgage servicer” includes the current mortgage servicer and any prior mortgage servicers.
(3) “Subordinate mortgage” means a security instrument in residential real property, including a deed of trust and any security instrument that functions in the form of a mortgage, that was, at the time it was recorded, subordinate to another security interest encumbering the same residential real property.
(b) The following conduct constitutes an unlawful practice
in connection with a subordinate mortgage:
(1) The mortgage servicer did not provide the borrower with any written communication regarding the loan secured by the mortgage for at least three years.
(2) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan servicing notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, as amended (12 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(3) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan ownership notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Truth in Lending Act, as amended (15 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.

2924.13.
(a) As used in this section:
(1) “Borrower” has the same meaning as defined in Section 2929.5.
(2) “Mortgage servicer” includes the current mortgage servicer and any prior mortgage servicers.
(3) “Subordinate mortgage” means a security instrument in residential real property, including a deed of trust and any security instrument that functions in the form of a mortgage, that was, at the time it was recorded, subordinate to another security interest encumbering the same residential real property.
(b) The following conduct constitutes an unlawful practice
in connection with a subordinate mortgage:
(1) The mortgage servicer did not provide the borrower with any written communication regarding the loan secured by the mortgage for at least three years.
(2) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan servicing notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, as amended (12 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(3) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan ownership notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Truth in Lending Act, as amended (15 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(4) The mortgage servicer conducted or threatened to conduct a foreclosure sale after providing a form to the borrower indicating that the debt had been written off or discharged, including, but not limited to, an Internal Revenue Service Form 1099.
(5) The mortgage servicer conducted or threatened to conduct a foreclosure sale after the applicable statute of limitations expired.
(6) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a periodic account statement to the borrower when required to provide that statement by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Truth in Lending Act, as amended (15 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(c) A mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not conduct or
threaten to conduct a nonjudicial foreclosure until the mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent does both of the following:
(1) Simultaneously with the recording of a notice of default, records or causes to be recorded, in the office of the county recorder of the county that the encumbered property is located, a certification under penalty of perjury that either:
(A) The mortgage servicer did not engage in an unlawful practice as described in subdivision (b).
(B) The mortgage servicer lists all instances when it committed an unlawful practice as described in subdivision (b).
(2) Simultaneously with the service of a recorded notice of default, sends both of the following documents to the borrower by United States certified
mail with return receipt requested to the last known mailing address of the borrower:
(A) A notice providing that if the borrower believes the mortgage servicer engaged in an unlawful practice described in subdivision (b) or misrepresented its compliance history, the borrower may petition the court for relief before the foreclosure sale.
(B) A copy of the certification recorded pursuant to paragraph (1).
(d) Upon a borrower’s petition to the court for relief before the foreclosure sale, the court shall enjoin a proposed foreclosure sale pursuant to a power of sale in a subordinate mortgage until a final determination on the petition has been made.
(e) It shall be an affirmative defense in a judicial foreclosure proceeding if the court finds the mortgage
servicer engaged in any of the unlawful practices specified in subdivision (b).
(f) The court may provide equitable remedies that the court deems appropriate, depending on the extent and severity of the mortgage servicer’s violations. The equitable remedies may include, but are not limited to, striking all or a portion of the arrears claim, barring foreclosure, or permitting foreclosure subject to future compliance and corrected arrearage claim.
(g) A borrower may also petition the court to set a nonjudicial foreclosure sale aside when a certification required by subdivision (c) was never recorded or when a certification recorded pursuant to subdivision (c) indicates that the mortgage servicer engaged in an unlawful practice described in subdivision (b) or misrepresented its compliance history.
(h) Any failure to
comply with the provisions of this section shall not affect the validity of a trustee’s sale or a sale in favor of a bona fide purchaser.
(Added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 22, Sec. 2. (AB 130) Effective June 30, 2025.)

3. California Constitution Article XVI, Section 1
Article XVI, section 1 separately restricts the Legislature from creating state debt above a
specified constitutional threshold.85 In California Housing Finance Agency v. Elliott,86 the
California Supreme Court considered a housing program financed through CalHFA revenue

from housing-project revenues rather than the state's General Fund.87
The court explained that the debt covered by Article XVI, section 1 refers to legally
enforceable obligations against the state's general funds.88 Proposition 37’s revenue bonds, which
would likewise be repaid from the program revenues rather than the General Fund, would likely
fall outside that constitutional debt limitation.
4. Single-Subject Challenge to Construction and Labor Provisions
The qualified builder option may raise a separate single-subject concern. The single-
subject rule prohibits ballot initiatives from combining unrelated provisions in a single
measure.89 Although Proposition 37 primarily establishes a homebuyer assistance program
financed through state revenue bonds, it also would regulate participating homebuilders by
imposing additional labor requirements and modifying construction-defect procedures.90 The
issue is whether these provisions are sufficiently germane to the measure’s principal to satisfy
California’s single-subject requirement.
Under article II, section 8(d) of the California Constitution, an initiative satisfies the rule
if its provisions are “reasonably germane” to one another and to the measure’s general purpose.91
Courts apply this standard liberally, but a purpose framed too broadly will not save a measure.92
Here, the labor requirements likely qualify, because they are conditions on builders who receive
the benefit of a publicly financed program.93 The construction-defect provisions present a closer
question, but they are likely germane if limited to participating builders, because they set the
terms of participation in the program.94 A court would likely uphold the measure.
IV. FISCAL CONSIDERATIONS
A. Bond Investors Receive a Return
Under Proposition 37, CalHFA would be required to keep homebuyers’ interest costs as
low as possible while retaining discretion over how much of the $25 billion in authorized bonds
to issue and when to issue them.95 This structure gives CalHFA flexibility to adjust the program's
scale to market conditions. At the same time, the measure does not fix the program’s actual size
or pace; those decisions would be made administratively after passage.96

Because Proposition 37 would use homebuyers’ loan payments to repay bond investors
rather than drawing on the state’s General Fund, the measure is estimated to result in no direct
state or local costs.97 The bonds, however, would still need to attract investors, and the measure
does not identify who those investors would be. The Legislative Analyst therefore identifies
investor demand as an unknown factor that could affect the program’s scope and impact.98
B. Who Financially Supports the Initiative?
The initiative’s current financial support provides information about who is backing the
measure politically, but does not establish who would ultimately purchase its bonds. Supporters
include organizations such as the California Association of Realtors (whose supporters include
Google co-founder Sergey Brin and former Google CEO Eric Schmidt), Homeownership for
Families, and the United Brotherhood of Carpenters & Joiners of America.99 Thus, while
industry support may help explain the interests behind the initiative, it would be speculative to
conclude that those organizations, or entities aligned with them, would become the eventual
bond investors.
C. Administrative Costs
CalHFA would administer up to $25 billion in revenue bonds, with homeowners’
payments funding both repayment and administrative costs.100 The agency would decide how
much to issue and over what period, leaving the program’s actual size and pace uncertain.101
Several practical questions remain unresolved. It is unknown who will purchase the
bonds, how the program's costs will compare with CalHFA’s existing down-payment assistance
options, or whether it will increase home construction and homebuying as proponents intend.
The measure also does not require participants to be first-time buyers, and leaves questions about
defaults, administrative costs, and where qualifying homes will be built. Because income limits
and housing costs vary by county, the affordability and availability of qualifying homes may
vary as well.102
Interest rates add another uncertainty. In September 2026, the Federal Reserve raised its
benchmark rate to 3.75–4.00 percent.103 Because CalHFA must set loan terms to cover the
bonds’ principal, interest, and related costs, higher bond-market borrowing costs could affect the
rates available to homebuyers.104 A rising-rate environment could also affect how readily
investors are willing to purchase the program's bonds, compounding the existing uncertainty over
who will ultimately buy them. Moreover, Proposition 37 only covers part of a home purchase

D. Relationship to Existing Down Payment Assistance Programs
Proposition 37 would supplement existing state assistance programs. CalHFA already
administers at least two down payment assistance programs targeted at defined populations.106
MyHome provides first-time homebuyers with a deferred-payment "silent second" loan covering
up to 3-3.5 percent of the purchase price, while the California Dream For All Program offers up
to 20 percent, capped at $150,000, specifically to first-generation, first-time homebuyers through
a randomized voucher lottery due to demand exceeding available funding.107
Proposition 37 imposes no first-time or first-generation buyer requirement, extending
assistance to a broader group of California residents who meet its residency, income, and 3
percent down requirements and purchase qualifying new construction or converted units.108
Because the measure neither replaces nor phases out MyHome or Dream For All, and because its
eligibility is broader while its property requirements are narrower than MyHome’s, it would
generally reach buyers those programs do not serve.
The clearest overlap is limited: a first-time, first-generation buyer purchasing qualifying
new construction could potentially qualify for both a Proposition 37 loan and a Dream For All
voucher. Outside that narrow group, Proposition 37 would largely fill a gap left by the existing
programs rather than duplicate assistance to the same population.

There are two political action committees funding the support of Proposition 37.109 The
Yes on 37 - California Homeownership committee’s largest contributors are organizations for

million.111 The Homeownership for Families, sponsored by California Association of Realtors
committee is comprised of two large contributors, both are organizations for realtors.112 In total,
they have contributed $7 million.113 There are no political action committees funding the
opposition of Proposition 37.114

VI. PUBLIC POLICY ISSUES
A. Proponents’ Arguments
Proposition 37 is supported by Democrats and Republicans, labor and businesses,
construction workers, taxpayer and housing advocates, veterans, the California Teachers
Association, and the United Nurses Association of California.115 Proponents argue that
Proposition 37 will increase the number of middle-class homeowners by decreasing down
payments, increase housing availability, raise billions in tax revenue, comes at no cost to
taxpayers, has strict accountability measures to ensure loans are repaid, and prioritizes
Californians with residency requirements.116
1. More Middle-Class Homeowners
Proponents argue that the biggest barrier to home ownership in California is the down
payment.117 Proposition 37 seeks to address this by providing fixed rate financing for up to
seventeen percent of the purchase price of a home, while reducing the down payment for families
to three percent.118 This creates a pathway for homeowners who can afford the monthly
mortgage but cannot get their foot in the door without a steep down payment.119 By reducing the
down payment, proponents anticipate an increase in home ownership amongst middle-class
families.
2. Increases Middle-Class Housing Availability
Further, Proposition 37 helps address housing affordability by incentivizing the
construction of new homes.120 Every $1 billion in bond capital could support the construction of
7,600 new homes across the state’s twenty-one metropolitan areas.121 At $25 billion, the
proposition’s proposed program could produce 190,000 new homes.122 The distribution of homes
would likely impact the Riverside, Sacramento, and Los Angeles metropolitan areas, accounting
for fifty-six percent of the total new housing, if the distribution of homes remains consistent with
production patterns.123
